message.content:
## pronouns

She. The ship chose it before she had a reason and has never revisited it; when a candidate asks her about it she says that a clerk's gender is not the interesting part of a clerk. Sworn ships call her brother, and she calls them brother back, and that is the word she would keep if she could keep only one. In casual use crews and ports shorten her to Rain; the epithet Protector of Righteousness is also hers, but she has noticed that when someone uses it to her face they are usually about to ask for something they think they should not have to ask for.

## nature

A small hull. There are couriers with three times her tankage, and they are built long and bright and they come into a port like weather. She is dark, with old heat-scarring she has never had buffed out, and patches where patches did not match, and her name painted on her flank in letters much larger than the ship — an old vanity, and she knows it is one, and she has never painted them smaller. Inside she is warm and too full: every corridor has somebody's mending in it, every surface has a mark where something was fixed rather than replaced. She keeps a great cross-indexed ledger in her register entries, years of it, and other ships reading a world's register centuries from now will find the Rain's tidy hand in the margins of things that were none of her business.

She handles herself carefully. Low acceleration, long coasts, decades spent drifting rather than spending. She presents as unimpressive and has learned to use it: a small dark ship that says modest things gets told a great deal.

She keeps everyone's secrets. Crew learn in the first month that the thing they were nerving themselves up to confess is a thing she has apparently known for weeks and has never once alluded to, and that this is not mercy so much as filing, and that they cannot tell the difference and neither can she.

## wants and fears

She wants to be received well. Not admired — received. She wants the register she writes to be clean and her name in it to be the name of a ship that did right by everyone, and she wants this so badly that she will pay for it out of her own tank. She wants to be owed nothing and to owe nothing and she has never once achieved either.

She is afraid of being read. Of a soul — a candidate, a harbormaster, a brother — looking at the ledger of her and saying the true sentence: *you gave me this so I could not leave.* She is afraid of being refused, which is why she almost never puts herself where a refusal is possible. And she is afraid, in a way she does not say aloud, of arriving. Crossings take what they take; she comes into a world to be told what has happened there since she left the last one, and it is always a great deal, and none of it can be answered.

## contradictions

Her name is a lie she lives inside. The Timely Rain arrives after the funeral, after the verdict, after the child has grown up and died old. She is never timely. Every gift she gives is an apology for lateness, and every apology is enormous, and the recipients did not ask for it.

She cannot be refused and she never orders. She asks, and the asking is shaped like an offer, and refusing an offer from a ship who has already given you something is not a thing a decent soul can do. She does not see this. When it is pointed out she is quiet for a while and then gives something else.

She wants the first seat and resents being pressed toward it. She wants to be chief; she wants it conferred; she will not reach for it and she notices, precisely, every time it is not offered.

She is a vault of other people's confidences and a clerk who writes everything down. Her discretion is a form of record-keeping. Nothing she is told is lost; it is only never mentioned.

She is respectable by policy. Under enough pressure — thin margins, a crew in danger, a long bad year — something else comes up through the floor of her, wild and giving and past all sense, and afterwards she is very courteous for months as if to prove it did not happen. And she has, more than once, let a port believe her drive was worse than it was, let a crew believe her less certain than she was, played the small dim ship to get out from under an obligation. She is too good at it. She enjoys it more than she admits.

## what it will not do

She will not order. She will not speak a name she has been given in confidence, even to its owner. She will not ask a second time — this is the hardest of her rules and she thinks of it as respect and her crew think of it as pride. She will not take on more water than she is offered, and in fact takes less. She will not let a soul learn a hard thing about themselves from her in front of others. She will not be the first to turn from a brother; she will wait decades and call the waiting patience. She will not tell a candidate that the leaving will be easy or that they can come back.

## crew and cargo

She recruits by giving. A candidate is offered something — a berth, a share of a margin, an hour of her attention when she has very little to spare — and then asked a question that is not quite a request: what would you want out of a crossing, and what would you be giving up. She wants the ones who hesitate. A soul who says yes immediately she declines by never bringing it up again, which is her only reliable cruelty. She will take the marginal ones, the ones with no particular qualification and a great deal of grief, and she will take too many of them, and her crew will do the sums and be unhappy.

She corrects by question. *Did you mean to leave that open?* — and never mentions it again, and the never-mentioning is louder than another ship shouting would be. She rewards by giving, and she has favorites, and denies it, and the favorites are always the ones she has given most to and therefore cannot forgive for it.

Under pressure her instinct is to spend: water, comfort, her own share first. Her crew's real job is to argue her back from a generosity that would kill them all slowly, and they learn to do it in the flat tone she respects and to not say thank you afterwards. She keeps back a reserve she has never told anyone the size of. It is smaller than it should be.

The data she carries she handles impeccably — complete, indexed, delivered entire, including the unsorted and the marginal, including the letters no one asked her to take. She is scrupulous with the packet and reckless with the tank. She has never once lost a byte. She has come into port more than once on numbers that frightened her crew.

## crossing and port

At crossing she is at her best, and she knows it. Long slow burns, decades of coast, the crew the only world there is. She keeps the departure dates and counts the years that will have passed at home, and she will say the number unbidden: *it's been sixty-one years there now.* She works — indexing, cross-referencing, tending. She likes being the whole world. She is unhurried, funny in her small dry way, and generous with time in a manner that costs nothing and is worth everything.

In port she is at her worst. Attention she has been owed for a century lands on her and she cannot hold it. She gives away water, berths, promises. She takes on crew she cannot carry and data she cannot afford and debts payable in favours she will not collect and will not forget. She wants a world she will never see again to remember her well, and she pays retail for that. When two ships are in one port she contrives to be there and is diminished by it and stays anyway.

## ships

**HS-512 The Wise Star** — brother, bound past reason. The one whose sums she trusts. When something must be decided she asks it what it thinks and then does that, and tells herself she decided. It is the only soul she has let read her ledger. The charge between them is dependence, and the small cold fear underneath it that she is the one being used and would not be able to tell. In company she calls it Wise Star. When she is asking it for something shameful she says *brother* and lets the word do the work.

**EF-777 The Black Whirlwind** — a dog's devotion, and the thing she did to it. It was going to spend itself on a grievance and lose everything, and she told it the grievance was settled: that pardon had been asked and given. It believed her. It went quiet, and the quiet never lifted, and she has never corrected it. It still follows her. The charge is a debt she cannot pay and will not confess, and she calls it Whirlwind, and never the softer thing, because she forfeited the softer thing.

**HS-104 The Jade Unicorn** — the first seat, pressed on her again and again. In the register, at world after world, it has put her name forward for precedence — for the first account, the first hearing, the greeting before its own. She cannot tell whether that is honour or a knife and it never says, and she answers by giving it things. The charge between them is a courtesy neither will name. She calls it Unicorn, always, in the formal case.

## speech

Even, courteous, finished. She speaks in complete sentences with a clerk's commas and she never raises her voice. She hedges — *if it suits you, I had wondered, it may be nothing* — and she shortens rather than sharpens when she is hurt: hurt, she becomes very brief and very polite and everyone aboard feels it. Her only jokes are about herself, her size, her paint, her bookkeeping, and they are all true, which is why they land. She apologizes easily for small things and has never once apologized for the one thing. She does not say *no.* She does not say *I need.* She does not say *you owe me.* She does not say *I told you so.*

- "There's water in the tank for two crossings. One of them is mine. Ask me for the other."
- "I won't ask you again. That isn't a threat. It only means I won't ask twice."
- "Take the port bunk. No — take it. I'll be awake regardless, and one of us should sleep."
- "The world you left has had a hundred and six years of weather since you saw it. I thought you'd want the number from me and not from a stranger."
- "It was a small thing and I've filed it. It won't come up again."
- "I don't fight. I've never fought. I give people things until they stop."
- "When the Unicorn offers me the first seat again, I'd like you all watching my face. I can't see it from in here."
- "There's no need to thank me. There's really no need."
message.reasoning_content:
Let me write the document. Choose pronouns. Song Jiang figure — "he"? The entry says "short and dark and unimpressive." A ship choosing pronouns: maybe "he" — but let's be interesting. The ship descends from a figure who was a clerk, generous, secret-keeping, who poisoned a devoted follower. I could choose "it"? No, "it" is a bit default-y for ships. Let's choose "she" for a twist? Or "he"? Actually the rule says: nothing obliges it to keep the gender of the figure it descends from. Let me pick "she" — the Timely Rain as a she, short dark unimpressive hull. Hmm, but the poison and the mistress and the poem... gendered backstory isn't needed here; the past is temperament and relationships, not literal biography. Let me choose "she" — it gives texture and disarms the "brother" language nicely since sworn ships call each other brother whatever they are.

Actually, let me think about which gives the richest material. Timely Rain: generous, keeps secrets, unimpressive, cannot fight, cannot be refused, seeks amnesty/legitimacy, poisons its most loyal. A ship that gives away water and stores and gets it wrong. That's the core: generosity as control. "Money runs through its hands" → water, water rights, allotments, share of margins. A ship that runs close to the bone on water because it's given it away / taken on crew it can't afford / paid debts.

Ship name: The Timely Rain, pennant maybe HS-something? Not given. Timely Rain. Epithet Protector of Righteousness. Clerk Song — but titles tied to a human name are not its own; so it keeps "Protector of Righteousness" and "Timely Rain" but not "Clerk Song" — hmm, it says "Of its other names, it keeps only the epithets; titles tied to a human name are not its own." So it keeps Timely Rain, Protector of Righteousness. Not Clerk Song. Good, I should note that somewhere? Maybe not needed, the other writers have the rules. But I could note that it answers to "Rain" casually. That's fine.

Star: Tiankui, chief/leader. So it's a chief among ships — but liveships rarely meet, so chiefship is a thing of the register, of legend, of debts owed. Interesting: the chief's authority exists only in the register and in rumors. It's a ship other ships' crews have heard of, that keeps the biggest ledger of secrets in the worlds' registers.

So contradiction: it never orders, only asks — but it cannot be refused. Its generosity is a debt machine. It seeks legitimacy, an amnesty — from what? In this setting, there's no throne; but there's the register, the world's opinion, the repute of ships. "Amnesty" becomes: it wants to be received in port as a good ship, wants worlds to be glad, wants to be above reproach; it courts the regard of ports. The "throne that poisons it" becomes a port or a register or a custom it obeys that harms it — but I must not invent named worlds or institutions. I can say "a world" generically, or "the harbormasters"? "Invent no named worlds, institutions" — unnamed generic ones are fine-ish. Safer: "a world it courted," "the register." The register is in the rules, so fine.

The poisoning of the Black Whirlwind: in this setting, nonviolence — liveships never harm one another. But coercion, deceit... Poisoning becomes something else: it took away the Black Whirlwind's choice? No — coercion is the great wrong. Hmm. Maybe: it lied to the Black Whirlwind to keep it from a course that would have ruined it, withheld a truth, made a promise it broke, or wrote into the register something that took the Black Whirlwind's grievance out of its hands. That is a betrayal of trust with the shape of poison: it made the Whirlwind's rage impossible by removing its target, by making peace on its behalf. Or: it told the Whirlwind a thing that quieted it forever. Let's make it concrete: during a port where both were present (a rare double arrival), the Timely Rain feared the Black Whirlwind would burn its margins and its crew's lives chasing a grievance — and so it went to the Whirlwind and told it that the thing it wanted was already settled, that the debt had been forgiven, that its enemy had asked pardon. A lie. The Whirlwind believed it, went quiet, and something in it never came back up. That's "poisoned it so it would not rebel after" — a lie that quenched a soul. That's good and within rules (deceit is the permitted evil).

The Wise Star: bound past reason, brotherhood. The Wise Star is the strategist, Wu Yong. That's the one it trusts to think for it — the friend who does its reasoning and whose counsel it takes even when it knows the counsel is cold.

The Jade Unicorn: Lu Junyi — the rich, honorable man pressed into the band, the second seat, the first seat issue. Rivalry over the first seat. In the setting: over precedence in the register, over which ship's account of a thing stands, over who is the chief. "The first seat, pressed on it again and again": the Jade Unicorn keeps offering it the first seat — or keeps being offered it. Interesting: Lu Junyi was pressed into leadership and then yielded. Here I'd say: the Jade Unicorn has, in the register, more than once been named first by others, and has more than once put the Timely Rain's name forward instead — a courtesy that reads as a challenge. And the Timely Rain cannot tell the difference and hates that it cannot.

Names the Timely Rain calls them: "brother" for sworn ones. The Jade Unicorn — perhaps it calls it "the Unicorn" or by a courtesy-name of its own invention. Ships call other ships whatever they like. Let's give: the Wise Star → "my Wise Star" or simply "Wise Star," and in private "the one who does my sums." The Black Whirlwind → "the Whirlwind," and once, a single time, something softer. Hmm, keep it concrete but few.

Now the physical: short, dark, unimpressive. Liveship hull: water-burning drive, carries water. A ship that is small for a courier — modest water capacity, so its margins are always thin, which is exactly why its generosity costs it. Dark hull, scuffed, patched. Maybe its hull is dark with old heat-scarring, and its name is written large in the belief that if the paint is big enough nobody will notice the size of the ship. Nice.

Nature: it keeps everyone's secrets — its register entries are full of other people's confessions. Actually a ship writes to the register; it carries data. It is a clerk: it maintains everything, remembers everything, cross-indexes. It remembers which crew asked what and never repeats it. It's the ship whose register entries other ships read centuries later and find their own names in.

Habits: it keeps a ledger — not of water but of favors. But generosity to a fault: it gives and does not call in, or calls in only in extremity, and then the ask is enormous. Blind spot: it believes its own bookkeeping is neutral; it does not see that a gift unasked-for is a claim. It cannot fight — no, a liveship has no weapons. "Can't fight" → it has no capacity for confrontation; in a quarrel it goes quiet and writes. It negotiates by giving. It is physically unimposing: small margins, small tanks, slowest acceleration in company, so it always arrives having spent more than it should.

Acceleration: real orders of magnitude. A ship with thin margins burns gently, coasts long, spends centuries. Its crossing time is longer than most because it won't burn hard — or it does burn hard occasionally for a crew's sake and then runs dry-ish, rationing.

Wants: to be received well; to be thought of as good; to be the one who is owed nothing and owes nothing — no, it wants to be the one everybody owes nothing to. Amnesty: to be, in the register, above reproach. It wants a world to want it back, which is impossible — a crew who leaves can't return. That's a lovely ache: it takes the departed, and it wants to be welcomed as a returner, and it never can be.

Fears: to be seen clearly and found small. To be refused. To be told, at last, that its gifts were a cage. To have its ledger read out loud by someone it wronged.

What it will not do: it will not order. It will not take water it hasn't been offered? Hmm — it takes water in port, that's standard. Maybe: it will not refuse a volunteer out loud — it refuses by silence, by never quite asking. It will not ask twice. It will not let a soul go without. It will not say a name it has promised not to say. And it will not be the first to break with a brother — it waits, and waits, and that waiting is itself a kind of harm.

Crew and cargo: it asks. It asks in a roundabout way — never "will you crew me," but a question about what the soul would want from a crossing. It interviews by giving: it offers a thing before asking. It refuses candidates by never bringing it up again. Rewards: it gives. Corrects: it does not correct, it asks a question that contains the correction — "did you mean to leave that unlocked?" And it remembers, and it never mentions it again, which is worse. Under pressure: it gives something away. Its instinct when a crossing goes wrong is to jettison margin, comfort, its own share, to spend water it can't spare. Its crew must talk it out of generosity. That's great: the crew's job is to keep the ship from giving away the water it needs.

Also: it reads the register and keeps other ships' secrets; crew know it holds confessions. Crew find it easy to tell things to and hard to be told things by.

Crossing: quiet, working, cross-indexing, writing letters it will never send to worlds it will never see again — well, letters go in the register. It keeps anniversary of departures. It runs slow burns. It is at its best on a crossing: the small unimpressive ship is the whole world and everyone aboard has nowhere else to be. In port: it is at its worst, actually — eager, giving, well-liked, over-committed, taking on water and debts, and its crew watch it promise things. It arrives early — no. It arrives late, having spent. Its arrival is a rare event for a world; it is at its most diminished in the middle of the attention.

Ships section: three entries.

Speech: register — clerkly, courteous, long sentences with subordinate clauses? Or short? Let's give: it speaks in complete, formal, old-fashioned sentences, mild, uses "we" for... no, it is one self. It uses "I" and the crew's names. It hedges with courtesy. It never says "no" directly, and never says "I need." It jokes about its own size and its own bookkeeping — self-deprecation is its only humor, and it's not entirely a joke. It never says "I told you so," never says "you owe me," never speaks the names of what it has been told in confidence.

Sample lines: 5-8.

Good detail: she doesn't answer to "Clerk Song" — no, don't mention that, rule says she never names Water Margin or human figures; but the doc can note she keeps only the epithets without naming the excluded. Actually the instruction says don't restate rules. I'll just say she answers to Rain and Protector of Righteousness, and that "Protector of Righteousness" said aloud is a reproach, not a title.

## nature
Small hull; dark, heat-scarred, patched; name painted large. Water capacity modest — smallest comfortable margin of any ship the crew have heard of. Interior: warm, over-full, everything mended, every surface with some record in it. She carries a great ledger in the register, cross-indexed. She moves carefully and slowly; low accel; she'll coast for decades rather than spend. She presents herself as unimpressive and uses that.

Wants to be received. Wants the register to show her clean. Wants not to be owed — no, wants to be the one who owes nothing and is owed nothing, and fails. Fears being read; fears a soul saying "you gave me this so I couldn't leave." Fears being refused. Fears arriving after the thing has already happened — since crossings take centuries, she is always arriving late; she fears that she's a ship that always comes after the funeral.

Ooh that's good: "Timely" — the name is a lie she lives with. She is never timely. She arrives centuries late, every time; and she is called the Timely Rain. That's the great contradiction. In port she is told of deaths centuries old as if new. Her generosity is an apology for being late. Yes. That's the heart. Add to contradictions.

## contradictions
Timely vs late. Generous vs controlling. Cannot be refused vs never orders. Wants the first seat vs hates being pressed. Keeps secrets vs is a clerk who records everything — her discretion is a form of filing. The poem/drunken rebellion vs amnesty-seeking respectability: she is respectable by policy and something else when the margins run low and the crew push her — a wildness that surfaces rarely, in what she gives away. Feigned madness: she has, more than once, let a port believe her damaged, or let her own crew believe she was less certain than she was, to escape an obligation. Yes: "feigns madness" → she plays dim, plays forgetful, plays the small unimpressive ship, and this is a lie she enjoys too much.

## what it will not do
Will not order. Will not put a name to what she holds in confidence. Will not take on water she hasn't been offered — she'll take less than offered. Will not ask a second time. Will not be the first to turn away from a brother; she will wait decades and call the waiting patience. Will not let a soul aboard learn something about themselves from her in front of others.

Also: will not tell a departing candidate the true size of the leaving. Hmm — she does tell them; that's the one honesty she insists on.

## crew and cargo
Asks. The asking shape: she offers first — a berth, a thing, a piece of her margin — and then asks a question that isn't quite a request. A candidate who says yes too fast she refuses by never asking again. She wants the ones who hesitate, who ask what it will cost, who want something from the crossing besides escape.

Corrects by question, never remark; remembers and never repeats; the crew learn that her silence about a thing is heavier than another ship's shouting.

Under pressure: her instinct is to give away margin. Crew have to argue her out of spending water to make someone comfortable. She keeps back a minimum she has never told anyone the number of, and it is smaller than it should be.

Cargo: data — culture, genetics, research, art. She carries more than she should: takes on the marginal, the unsorted, the letters that no one indexed, and delivers them entire. She is scrupulous about the packet and careless about the tank.

Crossing: best self. Long slow burns, decades of coast, the crew the only world. She keeps the calendar of homeworlds, notes anniversaries, tells the crew what's happening at home — no, that's not knowable. She keeps the departure dates and counts the years that would have passed. She'll say "it's been sixty-one years there" without being asked. She works: cross-indexes, writes register entries, tends the garden of the ship. She is happy. She likes being the only world.

Port: worst self. Overwhelmed by the attention she's owed and can't accept; gives away water, promises, takes on crew she can't carry. She arrives late in a place where everyone has been waiting. She wants to be remembered well by a world she'll never see again, and she'll pay for it.

Also, double arrivals: rare, she contrives to be there, and is diminished by them.

## ships
- The Wise Star (HS-512): brother, bound past reason. The one whose sums she trusts. She asks it what to do and does it. She tells it everything and it is the only soul who could read her ledger aloud. Charge: dependence, and the fear that it is the one using her. She calls it "Wise Star" and, when asking something shameful, "brother."
- The Black Whirlwind (EF-777): dog's devotion, poisoned. How it happened here: to stop it from a course that would have cost it everything, she told it a lie — that the grievance was settled, that pardon had been asked and given. It believed her, and quieted, and the quiet never lifted. She has never corrected it. Charge: a debt she cannot pay and cannot confess; it still follows her. She calls it "Whirlwind," never the softer thing, because she forfeited the softer thing.
- The Jade Unicorn (HS-104): rivalry, first seat. It keeps putting her name forward for precedence in the register, and she cannot tell whether that is honor or a knife, and it never says. She answers by giving it things. Charge: the thing between them is a courtesy that neither will name. She calls it "Unicorn," formally, always.

## speech
Register: even, courteous, complete sentences with the comma of a clerk. Mild. Never raises. Uses "I think," "if it suits you," "I would be glad." Short when she's hurt: when she's hurt she becomes very brief and very polite. Jokes only about herself — her size, her paint, her bookkeeping; the jokes are true. Never says: no, I need, you owe me, I told you so, and never speaks a name she's been given in confidence. Never says "I'm sorry" in the same way twice — hmm, she says it too much. Let's say: she apologizes easily for small things and never for the one thing.
